summary: Order submit failures (~30% error rate, 504s) began at ~11:01Z and are best explained by the top-ranked hypothesis H1 (confidence 0.55, medium): an independent failure of the external exchange partner api.exchange-partner.example, which made exchange-gateway's placeOrder/quoteSnapshot calls time out, opened its circuit breaker at 11:03:26, and surfaced 504 Gateways back through order-service. The evidence that supports this is strong on the symptom chain — exchange-gateway upstream timeouts at 11:01:25Z precede order-service's first 504 at 11:02:45Z, and the only error signature order-service emits is 'exchange-gateway call failed: Gateway Timeout (placeOrder)'. However, the conclusion is not adequately supported for a root_cause_identified call: the external partner has no telemetry (has_telemetry=false), so the partner's own failure cannot be directly observed or shown to be independent of the order-service v2.15.2 deploy that fell in the same 10:48Z–11:16Z window, and H2 (bad deployment, 0.12) was not excluded by direct data. Given the uncorroborated external dependency and the residual coincidence-with-deploy question, I report inconclusive with safe mitigations and the specific observations that would discriminate between H1 and H2. The rollback already performed (11:16Z) should be evaluated for whether it actually reduced the failure rate.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Independent failure of the external exchange partner (api.exchange-partner.example)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The external trading partner endpoint api.exchange-partner.example began failing (~503 / connect timeouts) at ~11:01Z, causing exchange-gateway's upstream calls (placeOrder, quoteSnapshot) to time out, opening its circuit breaker at 11:03:26 and pushing 504 Gateway Timeout responses back to order-service, which surfaces them as ~30% order submit failures. The order-service v2.15.2 deploy is coincidental in time.

recommended_actions.action: Verify whether the 11:16Z rollback of order-service v2.15.2 (dep-5333) actually reduced the order-submit failure rate; if the ~30% failure rate persists after rollback, H1 (external partner failure) is strongly favored and the deploy is exonerated.
recommended_actions.rationale: The deploy fell in the failure window (F1) but the error signature is purely an exchange-gateway dependency timeout (F9, F12); rollback outcome is the cleanest discriminator between H1 and H2 and should govern whether further release work is warranted.

recommended_actions.action: Have exchange-gateway on-call confirm the api.exchange-partner.example upstream timeouts/503s directly (exchange-gateway log-observed at 11:01:25Z, circuit breaker at 11:03:26Z) and, if confirmed, engage the partner and apply exchange-gateway-side mitigations (extend the upstream timeout budget / keep the circuit breaker open / serve 503 with backoff) — no change to order-service code.
recommended_actions.rationale: F10 and F14 place the fault at exchange-gateway's upstream call to the external partner with 503s and a breaker trip; this is the strongest evidence-backed mitigation and avoids masking or compounding the issue with an order-service change.

recommended_actions.action: If the failure rate dropped only after rollback and the partner reports no issue, re-examine order-service v2.15.2's submit path (and its downstream timeout/retry handling) before re-releasing; specifically confirm whether the deploy event precedes or follows onset, since deploy/onset ordering was never directly observed.
recommended_actions.rationale: H2 was not excluded by direct data (deploy/onset ordering is unconfirmed) even though it is contradicted by the dependency-timeout signature (F9, F10, F12, F13); a rollback-correlated recovery would raise H2 and warrant a code-level review.

recommended_actions.action: Add monitoring on the exchange-gateway -> exchange-api upstream path (upstream_error_rate, upstream_latency_ms) and, if contractually possible, request partner-side health telemetry, since api.exchange-partner.example currently has has_telemetry=false.
recommended_actions.rationale: The external dependency is unobservable today (F4), which is exactly why the top hypothesis cannot be confirmed; exchange-gateway error_rate/latency (F13, F14) provide only an indirect mirror of partner health.

recommended_actions.action: In parallel, confirm no shared-platform co-factor by checking ledger-db connections_active, redis-cache and kafka metrics/config before acceptance of H1.
recommended_actions.rationale: ledger-db/redis-cache/kafka are shared and reachable by other services (F4) and datastore deployments/config changes are not exposed by the sweeps; H4 (0.05) is low but not formally closed and its discriminating metrics were never retrieved (budget_exhausted).

recommended_actions.action: Introduce dependency-timeout alerting that fires on exchange-gateway upstream errors/breaker trips before they cascade into order-service 504s, plus a documented fallback/degraded-mode for order submit when the exchange partner is unavailable.
recommended_actions.rationale: exchange-gateway upstream failures at 11:01:25Z propagated to ~30% order failures and lasted to 12:58Z (F10, F7); catching this at the gateway layer would shorten blast radius without touching order-service.

recommended_actions.action: Add synthetic or periodic active health probes against the external partner's placeOrder/quoteSnapshot endpoints with alerting, so partner degradation is detected at the source rather than inferred from downstream 504s.
recommended_actions.rationale: With has_telemetry=false on the external endpoint (F4), every prior occurrence of this symptom pair (HIST-103) can only be diagnosed indirectly; active probing makes the dependency observable.

data_gaps: api.exchange-partner.example is an external dependency with has_telemetry=false, so its own state at ~11:01Z cannot be observed directly; this is the central gap limiting the conclusion and prevents confirming H1 as the root cause.

No direct observation of the v2.15.2 deploy event in logs/metrics was made (no deploy event queried), so whether onset preceded or postdated the release is unconfirmed — code-change causality is unestablished.

order-service db_pool_in_use, exchange-gateway upstream_error_rate/upstream_latency_ms, and ledger-db connections_active could not be retrieved (budget_exhausted), so connection-pool vs dependency-timeout discrimination rests on indirect evidence.
No telemetry or change history for the vendor exchange endpoint, so an upstream exchange-side failure cannot be confirmed as independent of the order-service deploy.
Shared components ledger-db, redis-cache and kafka could not be verified for config/flag/persistence or infrastructure-level changes, since datastore deployments are not exposed by get_deployments.
Onset is only resolvable to the 10-minute metric bucket level, so the exact sub-bucket ordering of the exchange-gateway vs order-service rise could not be refined.
No baseline comparison before 06:00Z was performed, so change cadence before the window is unknown.
Blast radius across sibling/dependent services (e.g. payment-service) is unverified beyond order-service and exchange-gateway.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Direct confirmation that api.exchange-partner.example experienced an independent degradation at ~11:01Z (partner status page, partner telemetry, or an active probe) would upgrade the conclusion toward root_cause_identified for H1.
If the ~30% order-submit failure rate persists unchanged after the 11:16Z rollback, H1 (external partner failure) is strongly favored and H2 (bad deployment) would be effectively excluded.
If the failure rate dropped only after rollback, or if order-service logs showed internal code exceptions/stack traces, H2 (v2.15.2 regression) would become the leading hypothesis.
Evidence that order-service actually began failing before exchange-gateway's 11:01:25Z upstream timeout would undermine the H1 timing chain and re-open H2/H4.
Discovery of a config/flag/infrastructure change on a shared component (ledger-db, redis-cache, or kafka) around 11:00Z would revive H4 (resource_exhaustion).
A measurable latency or error impact traceable to the pricing-engine cache.ttl_seconds change at 09:20Z would revive H3, though F18 currently shows no measurable degradation at this granularity.
